title: California's AI provenance law hits large gen-AI providers — SB 942 becomes operative with $5,000-per-day penalties
subtitle: Any generative-AI system with more than a million monthly California users now owes C2PA-compatible provenance on every image, video and audio output, plus a free public detection tool.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: California's AI Transparency Act — SB 942 as amended by AB 853 — becomes operative on August 2, imposing content-provenance duties on any 'covered provider' of a generative AI system with more than one million monthly California users. Covered providers must embed a latent, C2PA-compatible provenance marker into every synthetic image, video and audio output; expose an optional visible manifest disclosure the user can add on request; and publish a free, public AI-detection tool that lets anyone check whether a piece of content came from the provider's model. Violations are enforced by the California Attorney General at $5,000 per day per instance — a per-day, per-piece cadence that scales quickly against high-volume image and video generators.

The operative date was moved to August 2 by AB 853, signed by Governor Newsom in October 2025 and deliberately synced to the EU AI Act's own August-2 milestones. The original operative date was January 1, 2026, and providers spent the intervening seven months building the manifest, latent-marker and detection-tool infrastructure. Scope is developer-side: SB 942 targets the entities that create or code the underlying generative AI system, not the businesses that deploy it inside their own products. That distinction is intentional. Sacramento's theory of the case is that provenance is a supply-chain problem best solved at the model layer, before content propagates through downstream apps.

The technical spine is C2PA — the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity standard co-authored by Adobe, Microsoft, the BBC and others. Latent markers must be machine-readable and reasonably resistant to normal editing operations; the manifest is the human-readable side of the same record, listing provider identity, model version, generation timestamp and any post-generation edits. California is the first US jurisdiction to make a specific technical standard the default expectation in state law, and the practical effect for consumers is that a growing share of AI-generated images and video circulating on US platforms will now carry cryptographic provenance data that content-authenticity tools can read and display.

For learners: if you build with generative-AI APIs, check whether the providers you rely on have implemented C2PA output-side by today. Most large-model APIs already write the manifest and latent marker at generation time — you inherit compliance by default. If a smaller or open-weight provider you use doesn't ship provenance, the exposure falls to whoever is the 'covered provider' for the deployed model, which for open weights typically means the deployer that stood the model up as a service. The interesting long-run question is whether C2PA becomes the de facto global standard through California's market weight, the way earlier California disclosure laws (cookies, environmental warnings) propagated well beyond the state's borders.
